unit.title: Manage personal stress in the workplace

summary: This unit teaches you to recognise and manage stress at work, especially in a busy, hot fabrication workshop where a lapse of attention can cause an accident. You will learn what stress is, what causes it, and its physical, emotional, thinking and behaviour signs. You will learn healthy ways to cope, how to plan your time and speak up about your workload, where to get help, how to support others, and how to make and review a personal stress action plan.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It is about **managing your own stress at work**: noticing when pressure is becoming too much, dealing with it in healthy ways, and getting help early.

Stress matters in any job, but in a welding and fabrication workshop it is also a **safety** matter. The work involves arc light, hot metal, electricity, grinders, saws and heavy steel, often in heat and noise. A worker who is tired, worried or rushing is more likely to skip a safety step, forget PPE or misjudge a cut, and to hurt themselves or someone else.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme, and anyone starting work in a trade. You do not need any special knowledge; you need to be honest with yourself about how you are coping.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Say what stress is, how the body reacts to pressure, and the difference between helpful pressure and harmful stress.
Name the causes of stress at work and outside work, including workshop conditions such as heat and noise.
Spot the physical, emotional, thinking and behaviour signs of stress in yourself and others, and explain why stress is a safety risk.
Find your own triggers and early warning signs, using a stress diary.
Use exercise, sleep, food and water, relaxation, talking and helpful thinking, and avoid unhealthy habits that make stress worse.
Plan your work, set priorities, and speak up calmly and assertively when there is too much to do.
Know where to get help at the Centre, at work and outside, when to see a professional, and how to support a co-worker.
Write a personal stress action plan with SMART goals, and review it.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on what stress is, its causes, signs and effects, healthy and unhealthy ways of coping, time management, communication, getting help, the workplace's part and action plans.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact words and figures, such as adrenaline, stressor, resilience, dehydration, fatigue, EAP, SMART) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks** in a group: a stress-awareness poster and a 10-minute toolbox talk for the welding workshop; then role plays of workplace scenes and a written stress action plan.

blocks.note: Nobody has to share private matters in this unit. For the action plan and the role plays, you may write about a made-up worker. If the topic upsets you, you can step out and speak to your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Stress** is the way your body and mind react when the demands on you feel greater than your ability to cope. Everybody feels it at times. It is not a sign of weakness or laziness, and it is not only a problem for managers: trainees, welders, stylists and electricians all feel it.

blocks.h: The body's alarm: fight or flight

blocks.p: When your brain senses danger or pressure, it sets off an automatic reaction called **fight or flight**. Hormones, mainly **adrenaline** and **cortisol**, are released into the blood to get you ready for action.

head: What happens in the body
Why
rows: Heart beats faster and harder; blood pressure rises
To pump more blood to the muscles
Ready to move, push or run
Sugar is released into the blood
To cool the body and save energy for action
Senses sharpen; the mind narrows onto the threat

blocks.p: This reaction is useful in real danger, such as jumping back from a falling sheet of steel. The problem comes when it is switched on day after day by deadlines, conflict or worry, and never has a chance to switch off. Then it wears the body and mind down.

head: Helpful pressure (positive stress)
Harmful stress (distress)
rows: Feels like a challenge you can meet
Passes when the task is done
Example: a fair deadline to finish a gate by Friday
Too much, for too long, or out of your control
Feels like a threat you cannot meet
Makes you tired, tense and unable to concentrate
Example: doing two people's work every day, with constant shouting and money worries at home

head: Amount of pressure
How you work
rows: Tired, anxious, making mistakes; in the end ill or burnt out

blocks.p: The things or events that cause stress are called **stressors**. The same stressor can affect two people differently: one welder finds a tight deadline exciting, another finds it frightening. What matters is how much pressure **you** feel and how long it lasts.

blocks.note: You are the main person responsible for managing your own stress, with support from others: your family, your instructor or supervisor, your employer and, when needed, health professionals.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Cause
Examples in a workshop
rows: Three gates and two sets of grills promised to customers in the same week
Not knowing what is expected, or getting different orders from two people
No say over how the work is done, or over the hours
Arguments over tools and space; being picked on or mocked; favouritism
A new supervisor, a new rota, new machines, a move to another site
Fear of mistakes or of losing work
Worry about spoiling an expensive job, or about being laid off when business is slow
Heat, constant grinder noise, fumes, poor lighting, cramped space, long hours, shift work
Being given a job you have not been shown how to do

blocks.note: Jamaica's heat is a stressor in itself. A metal-roofed workshop can be well over 30 °C by midday, and welding PPE adds to the heat. Heat makes people tired, irritable and less able to concentrate, and dehydration makes it worse.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Problems at home do not stay at the gate. They follow you into the workshop and affect how well you cope.

ul: **Money:** bills, debt, rent, school fees, a family member losing their job.
**Family:** caring for children, sick or elderly relatives; arguments; a death in the family.
**Relationships:** a break-up, or trouble with a partner.
**Travel:** long, costly or uncertain journeys to work by route taxi or bus.
**Housing and community:** overcrowding, poor housing, worry about crime and safety.
**Health:** your own illness or a family member's.
**Big events:** a hurricane or flood, moving house, a new baby, starting a course.

blocks.p: Stress often comes from several causes at once. A welder with money worries, a long journey and a heavy week at work can reach breaking point over something small, such as a missing chipping hammer.
Stress shows in four ways: in the **body**, in **feelings**, in **thinking** and in **behaviour**. Everyone shows it differently, so learn your own signs, and notice changes in the people around you.

head: Type of sign
Examples
rows: Eating much more or much less
Finding it hard to make decisions
Rushing, skipping safety steps, forgetting PPE

blocks.p: A short spell of stress does little harm. Stress that goes on for weeks or months can damage both **physical health** and **mental health**.

ul: **High blood pressure** and a greater risk of heart disease and stroke. High blood pressure is common in Jamaica and often has no signs: get yours checked at a health centre or pharmacy.
A weaker **immune system**, the body system that fights illness, so you catch infections more easily.
Stomach and bowel problems, headaches, and back and neck pain.
Poor sleep and **fatigue**: a deep tiredness that makes it hard to concentrate and work safely.
**Anxiety** and **depression**.
**Burnout**: feeling worn out, drained and detached from work after long-term stress, so that even rest does not seem to help.
Trouble at home and at work: arguments, broken relationships, warnings, lost jobs.

blocks.p: A stressed worker may be tired, distracted or in a hurry. In a workshop, that can mean:

ul: Forgetting to lower the helmet, or to put on safety glasses before grinding.
Leaving hot metal unmarked, or a gas cylinder valve open.
Misjudging a cut on the guillotine or saw.
Taking a short cut with a guard or a lifting job.
Being slow to react when something goes wrong.

blocks.h: If stress is affecting your concentration

flow: Stop the task and make it safe: switch off the machine, close the cylinder valves, put the hot work down
Tell your supervisor or instructor honestly that you cannot focus
Take a short break somewhere cooler and quieter; drink water; breathe slowly
If needed, ask to move to a lower-risk task for a while
If it keeps happening, talk to someone about the cause and get support

blocks.note: Never carry on with hot work, a grinder or a machine when you are dizzy, exhausted or cannot concentrate. Telling your supervisor is not weakness: it is what a professional does.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Self-awareness** means knowing your own strengths, weak points, moods and reactions. The better you know your own **early warning signs**, the sooner you can act, before stress builds up.

ul: Some people get a headache or a tight jaw first.
Some stop sleeping well, or start waking at 3 a.m. and worrying.
Some become short-tempered with family or co-workers.
Some start drinking more coffee or energy drinks, or eating badly.

blocks.p: A **stress diary** is a simple record, kept for one or two weeks, of when you felt stressed, what caused it, how you felt and what you did. After a week or two, patterns show up: the same person, the same day, the same kind of job.

head: Date and time
What happened (the trigger)
How I felt (0–10) and the signs I noticed
What I did
Did it help?
rows: Told the gate must be ready by 3 p.m., not Friday
8: tight chest, snapped at the apprentice
No: made a mistake on a hinge

blocks.p: When you read the diary back, ask: What causes my stress most? When does it happen? What are my first signs? What did I do that helped, and what made it worse? The answers are the start of your action plan.

blocks.note: Keep the diary short and honest; a few lines a day is enough. You do not have to show it to anyone.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Healthy and unhealthy ways to cope

head: Method
How it helps
How to do it
rows: Burns off the energy that stress hormones build up, loosens tight muscles, and releases chemicals that lift mood and improve sleep
Walking, football, cricket, dancing, cycling, swimming. Health guides commonly advise at least **150 minutes** of moderate activity a week, for example 30 minutes on five days.
A rested body and mind think more clearly and cope better with pressure
Most adults need at least **7 hours** a night. Keep a regular bedtime; put the phone away an hour before; avoid caffeine late in the day.
Regular meals keep energy steady and avoid the tiredness and bad temper that come with hunger
Breakfast, then regular meals with fruit, vegetables and water; fewer sugary drinks and fried snacks; no skipping meals.
**Dehydration** (losing too much water) makes you tired, irritable, dizzy and less able to cope
Drink water regularly through the day, before you feel thirsty. In hot work many safety guides suggest about a cup (250 ml) every 15 to 20 minutes.
Slows the heart and calms the body's alarm
Breathe in slowly through the nose for about 4 counts, and out through the mouth for about 6, for two or three minutes. Or tense and then relax each muscle group in turn.
Sharing a problem eases the worry and helps you see a way forward
A friend, family member, instructor, pastor or counsellor
Gives the mind a rest from work
Hobbies, music, church and faith, family time, a walk by the sea
Gives back a feeling of control
To-do lists, priorities, breaking jobs into steps (see the next section)
Changes how big the problem feels
Focus on what you can control; take one step at a time; be realistic, not perfect

head: Unhelpful thought
More helpful thought
rows: "If I finish the hinges this morning, the gate can be painted after lunch."
"This weld went wrong. What can I change on the next one?"
"I can't change the deadline, but I can ask for help with the grinding."
"Who can help, and what can wait?"

blocks.p: **Resilience** is the ability to bounce back after hard times. It grows with good habits, support from others, and experience of getting through difficulties step by step.

blocks.h: Unhealthy ways and why they make stress worse

blocks.p: Unhealthy ways of coping may give quick relief, but they do not deal with the cause, and they bring new problems.

head: Unhealthy habit
Why it makes things worse
rows: Lifts mood for a short time, then leaves you lower, more anxious and sleeping badly. Can lead to dependence, money problems and family trouble. At work it slows reactions and judgement: accidents and lost jobs.
May seem to calm you, but affect memory, concentration and motivation, and can lead to dependence. Being under the influence at work is unsafe and against workplace rules.
Raises the heart rate and harms the heart and lungs; does not remove the cause
**Caffeine** makes you jittery and anxious and spoils sleep, so you are more tired the next day
Skipping meals or overeating junk food
Swings in energy and mood; harms health over time
Removes the support that helps you cope; problems seem bigger and loneliness grows
Working through every break and every night
Damages relationships at home and at work, which adds more stress

blocks.note: Healthy methods work more slowly than a drink or a smoke, but they last. The best plan uses several of them together, every day.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Much work stress comes from feeling there is too much to do and not enough time. Planning gives back a feeling of control.

flow: At the start of the day, write a **to-do list** of everything that must be done
Sort the tasks by how **urgent** and how **important** they are
Break big jobs into smaller steps you can tick off
Estimate how long each task will take, and leave some spare time for problems
Do the most urgent and important tasks first
Avoid distractions, such as your phone, while you work
If it still will not all fit, tell your supervisor early and agree the priorities

head: Task is ...
Urgent
Not urgent
rows: **Do it first.** A gate the customer collects at noon; a gas leak or other hazard
**Plan a time for it.** Practising for your assessment; servicing the welding machine; making a budget
**Deal with it quickly, or hand it on if you may.** Some calls and messages; a request that can wait an hour
**Drop it or leave it till later.** Scrolling social media; tidying something that is already tidy

blocks.note: Take your **breaks**. Short, regular breaks during a long welding job let you rest your eyes, drink water, cool down and come back alert. Working through them leads to mistakes.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: When you are asked to take on more than you can do, there are three ways to respond.

head: Style
What it sounds like
Result
rows: "All right, no problem", then staying late every night, or leaving the job undone
Stress builds; the supervisor does not know there is a problem
"That's not my job! Get somebody else!"
Conflict and bad feeling; the problem is not solved
"I want to help. I already have the two gates for Thursday. Which job should come first?"
The supervisor knows the facts; together you agree the priorities

blocks.p: Being **assertive** means saying what you need clearly and calmly, with respect for the other person. Use **"I" statements**, which describe the problem and how it affects you, instead of blaming: "I get held up when the grinder isn't returned", not "You always take the grinder". Speak in private, at a good time, and listen to the other side.

ul: Ask for the facts: what is changing, when, and how it affects you.
Say calmly what worries you, and suggest how it could work for you.
Give the change a fair try before judging it.
Avoid spreading rumours; they make everyone more anxious.

head: Where
Who
rows: Your instructor, the guidance counsellor, student support staff
Your supervisor; the **human resources (HR)** department; an **employee assistance programme (EAP)** if the employer has one: free, confidential counselling paid for by the employer
Family, trusted friends, a pastor or church group, community groups
A doctor at a health centre or private practice; a counsellor or psychologist; the mental health team at your parish health services
The staff handbook, or student support staff at the Centre, tell you what help is offered

ul: Stress has lasted for weeks and is not getting better.
It is affecting your sleep, eating, health or ability to work.
You feel low, hopeless or anxious most of the time.
You are relying on alcohol, ganja or other drugs to cope.
You are having thoughts of harming yourself.

blocks.note: If you or someone else has thoughts of self-harm or suicide, get help **at once**: tell someone you trust, contact a doctor, go to the nearest hospital, or call the emergency services (in Jamaica, 110 for an ambulance, 119 for the police). The Ministry of Health and Wellness also runs a mental health helpline; your instructor or counsellor can give you its current number.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Notice changes: a cheerful person gone quiet, more mistakes, lateness, snapping, drinking. Then:

flow: Find a quiet moment and ask privately, "Are you all right? You seem a bit down lately."
Listen without judging, interrupting or rushing to fix it
Show you care, and say it is fine to get help
Suggest someone who can help, such as the supervisor, the counsellor or a doctor, and offer to go with them
Keep what they tell you private, unless they or someone else may be in danger: then get help straight away, even if they asked you not to

blocks.p: Never tease a stressed person, tell the group about their problems, or tell them to "stop being silly".
Employers have a duty to look after the **occupational safety and health (OSH)** of their workers, and stress is part of health. A good employer or training centre:

ul: Plans fair workloads and realistic deadlines.
Gives clear instructions and training, so people know what is expected.
Listens to staff and consults them about changes before they happen.
Allows proper breaks and reasonable hours.
Keeps working conditions decent: ventilation, fans, drinking water, lighting, noise control.
Does not allow bullying, and deals with conflict fairly.
Offers support, such as a counsellor or an EAP, and tells staff about it.

blocks.note: If you are being bullied, keep a note of what happened, when and who saw it, and report it to your instructor or another staff member you trust. Do not fight back, and do not suffer in silence.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **stress action plan** is your own written plan for managing stress. It turns what you have learnt into steps you will actually take.

flow: Keep a stress diary for one or two weeks
Pick out your main causes of stress and your early warning signs
For each main cause, write a **SMART** goal and the steps to reach it
Add the healthy habits you will build into each day
Write down who can support you
Set a date to review the plan, usually after two to four weeks
Review it: what helped, what did not; change the plan; keep going

head: Letter
Means
Check
rows: Does it say exactly what I will do?
Can I tell whether I have done it?
Can I really do it, with what I have?
Does it deal with one of my main causes of stress?
Does it say when, or by when?

blocks.p: "Be less stressed" is not a SMART goal. "Walk for 30 minutes after work on Monday, Wednesday and Friday for the next four weeks" is.

head: Part of the plan
Example (a made-up trainee)
rows: Falling behind with vertical welds; money worries; late nights on the phone
Tight jaw, snapping at my brother, lying awake
Ask my instructor on Monday for extra practice time on vertical welds, and practise twice a week for a month
Make a simple budget with my mother this Sunday
Phone off and in bed by 10:30 p.m. on weeknights, starting tonight
Breakfast every day; water bottle at work; walk three times a week; cut energy drinks to one a day
My instructor; the guidance counsellor; my older sister
In three weeks: check the diary and the goals, and change what is not working

blocks.p: A **toolbox talk** is a short safety talk given to a group at the work area. For the practical you give a 10-minute talk on stress using your poster.

ul: Keep to one topic and a few clear points: what stress is, its causes, its signs, why it is a safety risk, ways to cope, where to get help.
Use plain words and real workshop examples.
Each member presents the section they wrote, in their own words.
Leave time for questions, and collect written feedback.
Keep personal details out of the poster and the talk.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can explain what stress is and describe the fight-or-flight reaction.
I can explain the difference between helpful pressure and harmful stress, with examples.
I can name common causes of stress at work and outside work, including workshop conditions.
I can describe physical, emotional, thinking and behaviour signs of stress.
I can explain the effects of long-term stress on health, and what burnout is.
I can explain why stress is a safety risk in a workshop, and what to do if I cannot concentrate.
I can use a stress diary to find my own triggers and early warning signs.
I can describe healthy ways to cope and explain how each helps.
I can explain why alcohol, drugs, smoking, caffeine and isolation make stress worse.
I can plan my work with a to-do list and sort tasks by urgency and importance.
I can speak up about my workload calmly and assertively, using "I" statements.
I can say where to get help, and when to get professional help.
I can support a co-worker who seems stressed, and know when to get help at once.
I can write and review a stress action plan with SMART goals.

terms: A hormone released quickly in danger or under pressure; it speeds up the heart and breathing
Saying what you need clearly and calmly, with respect for others
Feeling worn out and drained after long-term stress
The drug in coffee, tea and energy drinks; too much worsens anxiety and sleep
A stress hormone that stays raised when stress goes on for a long time
Losing too much water from the body
Employee assistance programme: free, confidential counselling paid for by an employer
Deep tiredness that makes it hard to concentrate and work safely
The body's automatic reaction to danger, getting it ready for action
Human resources: the department that deals with staff matters
The body system that fights illness; long-term stress weakens it
How well a person thinks, feels and copes with life
The ability to bounce back after difficult times
Knowing your own strengths, weak points, moods and reactions
Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound: a way to write goals
The body and mind's reaction when demands feel greater than your ability to cope
A record of when you felt stressed, what caused it, how you felt and what you did
A short safety talk given to a group at the work area
Having enough time for work, rest, family and interests

c1.title: A deadline week in Junction
c1.text: Andre, a welder at a small fabrication shop in Junction, St Elizabeth, has promised three gates and a set of grills to customers. A co-worker is off sick, the shop reaches 34 °C by noon, and Andre has worked until 9 p.m. for four nights in a row. He has headaches, is snapping at the apprentice, has burnt his hand twice this week, and is drinking four energy drinks a day "to keep going". His list for Thursday morning reads: finish the gate Mrs Reid collects at 10 a.m. today; tidy the steel rack; start the grills due next Wednesday; reply to a supplier's text about a new price list.

c2.title: Money worries for a trainee in Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: Jhenelle is a welding trainee at a training centre in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. Her mother has lost her job, the light bill is overdue, and Jhenelle has started working evenings at a cook shop. In class she is often tired, forgets steps she knows well, and twice this month she has left a gas cylinder valve open at the end of the day. She spends her breaks alone on her phone and has told nobody what is happening, because she feels ashamed.

c3.title: A new Saturday rota in Annotto Bay
c3.text: Tevin works at a steel fabrication yard in Annotto Bay, St Mary. A new foreman has changed the rota, and Tevin is now asked to work every Saturday, although he looks after his young son on Saturdays while his partner works. For two weeks he has lain awake most nights, his neck and shoulders are tight, and he dreads going to work. He has kept a stress diary for those two weeks: most entries are on Friday afternoons, when the Saturday list is posted.

c4.title: Handrails in the sun at Runaway Bay
c4.text: Sanjay is part of a team fixing steel handrails at a new hotel in Runaway Bay, St Ann. The work is in full sun, the hotel wants it finished before guests arrive on Sunday, and the team leader shouts at anyone he thinks is slow. When the leader shouts at him, Sanjay's heart pounds and his hands shake, and he keeps telling himself, "This job is going to be a disaster." By 2 p.m. on Thursday he has drunk only one bottle of water since 7 a.m., and he feels dizzy while welding on a raised platform.

c5.title: Assessment nerves in Lucea
c5.text: Akeem is a Level 2 welding trainee at a training centre in Lucea, Hanover. His practical assessment is in two weeks. He has been staying up past 2 a.m. on his phone, skipping breakfast, and says he "freezes" whenever the assessor watches him. His instructor has set a timed practice assessment for next Tuesday.

questions.q: Which fact in the case is the clearest sign that Andre's stress has become a safety risk?
o: He has promised three gates to customers
The shop reaches 34 °C by noon
He has burnt his hand twice this week
A co-worker is off sick this week
questions.why: The other three are causes of pressure. Two burns in one week show that tiredness and stress are already making him careless with hot metal, so he must act before a worse accident happens.

questions.q: What is the best advice about the energy drinks?
o: Switch to strong coffee, which gives a healthier lift
Keep them, since he needs the energy until the gates are done
Have them only in the evenings, when he is working late
Cut down and drink water: the caffeine is spoiling his sleep
questions.why: Caffeine and sugar give a short lift and then a drop, and too much makes people jittery, irritable and unable to sleep. Water, regular food and rest give steadier energy, especially in the heat.

questions.q: Which task on Thursday's list should Andre do first?
o: Tidy the steel rack so the shop is easier to use
Finish the gate Mrs Reid is collecting at 10 a.m.
Start the grills, as they are the biggest job
Reply to the supplier's text about the price list
questions.why: That task is both urgent and important: a customer is coming for it within hours. The grills are important but due next week, the text can wait or be passed on, and tidying can be planned for a quieter time.

questions.q: Which plan for the rest of the week best protects Andre's health and safety?
o: Work until midnight on Thursday to get well ahead for the weekend
Skip lunch on Thursday and Friday to save an hour on each day
Stop at a set time, sleep seven hours or more, take water breaks
Keep the same hours, then take a long weekend once it is all over
questions.why: Tired workers make mistakes, and two burns show it is already happening. Sleep, breaks and water keep him alert; if the work still cannot fit, he should tell the owner early so that priorities or dates can be agreed.

questions.q: Which of Jhenelle's signs is a "thinking" sign of stress?
o: Forgetting steps she knows well
Working evenings at a cook shop
The overdue light bill at home
Spending her breaks alone
questions.why: Stress affects concentration, memory and decisions, so well-known steps get missed. The bill and the evening job are causes (stressors), and spending breaks alone is a behaviour sign.

questions.q: Jhenelle feels too ashamed to tell anyone about the money problems. What is the most helpful first step?
o: Speak privately to the Centre's guidance counsellor
Stop coming to class until things are better at home
Tell the whole class so that they understand her
Keep quiet, so that nobody thinks she is weak
questions.why: Counsellors are there to help and keep what she says confidential, and may know of support with fees or other help. Dropping out or bottling it up makes things worse, and she need not share private matters with the class.

questions.q: Jhenelle is writing a stress action plan. Which of these is a SMART goal?
o: Stop worrying about money from now on, whatever happens
Be much less stressed than I am now by the end of term
Do a money plan with my mother every Sunday for a month
Get more sleep at night whenever I have the time for it
questions.why: A SMART goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. "Every Sunday for a month" says exactly what, when and for how long, so she can check whether she did it.

questions.q: Which two of Tevin's signs are physical signs of stress?
o: Dreading work and looking after his young son
Lying awake and a tight neck and shoulders
Lying awake at night and dreading going to work
A tight neck and the new rota for Saturdays
questions.why: Physical signs show in the body: poor sleep, tight muscles, headaches, an upset stomach. Dread is an emotional sign, and the rota and minding his son are causes.

questions.q: How should Tevin use what his stress diary shows?
o: Stop the diary, since it only makes him think about stress
Avoid reading the Saturday list on Fridays from now on
Take Fridays off sick so that the list cannot upset him
Plan a calm talk with the foreman about the Saturday rota
questions.why: The diary has found his main stressor. Dealing with the cause, by talking to the foreman about the rota and his childcare, does more than avoiding the list or taking sick days.

questions.q: Which reply to the foreman is assertive?
o: "All right, whatever you need," and then worry about it all week
"I can do two Saturdays a month; I mind my son on the others."
"You can't make me work Saturdays. Find somebody else to do it."
"Maybe," and then simply not turn up when the Saturday comes
questions.why: An assertive reply says clearly and calmly what he can do and why, and leaves room to agree a fair answer. Giving in builds stress, attacking the foreman builds conflict, and not turning up breaks trust.

questions.q: At night Tevin lies awake going over the week. Which habit is most likely to help him sleep?
o: A regular bedtime, with the phone put away an hour before
A few drinks of white rum just before bed to help him relax
Watching videos in bed until he starts to feel sleepy
A strong coffee after supper so he gets his chores done
questions.why: A regular routine and a calm hour before bed without screens help the body wind down. Alcohol gives broken, poor-quality sleep, and screens and caffeine keep the brain awake.

questions.q: When the team leader shouts, why does Sanjay's heart pound and his hands shake?
o: The heat has raised the level of sugar in his blood
Welding fume has built up around the raised platform
He did not eat enough breakfast before work that day
His body releases adrenaline, ready to fight or run
questions.why: The fight-or-flight reaction pumps adrenaline into the blood: the heart speeds up and the muscles tense, ready for action. It helps in real danger, but switched on all day it wears the body down.

questions.q: Which thought would help Sanjay most?
o: "Nothing I do on this job will matter, so there is no point trying."
"It is all the team leader's fault, and there is nothing I can do."
"If we finish the top rails today, Saturday is enough for the rest."
"I must weld every single rail myself, to be sure that it is right."
questions.why: Helpful thinking is realistic and focuses on what he can control, with a clear next step. Expecting disaster, blaming others or trying to carry everything alone all add to stress.

questions.q: Sanjay feels dizzy on the platform. What should he do?
o: Sit on the edge of the platform until the dizziness passes
Ask a co-worker to hold him steady while he finishes the rail
Stop, make it safe, climb down, and drink water in the shade
Finish the rail he is on, then rest once that part is done
questions.why: Dizziness on a platform can mean a fall, and in this heat he is probably dehydrated. Stop and make the work safe, get down, cool off, drink water and tell the team leader; get medical help if he does not recover quickly.

questions.q: Which plan for the next two weeks is most likely to help Akeem?
o: Practise each weld on a set timetable and be in bed by 11 p.m.
Practise only the welds he already finds easy, for confidence
Stay up later to study, and catch up on sleep after the test
Leave practice until the last few days so that it stays fresh
questions.why: Planned, regular practice of every weld, with enough sleep and a proper breakfast, builds both skill and calm. Cramming and lost sleep make freezing more likely, not less.

questions.q: How can next Tuesday's practice assessment help Akeem?
o: It only adds stress, so he should ask to be excused from taking it
It means the real assessment will count for less in his final result
It helps him only if he manages to pass it at the first attempt
It gives fair pressure and gets him used to being watched
questions.why: A fair, short-term deadline is positive pressure: it sharpens focus, and the feeling passes when the task is done. Practising while being watched also makes the real assessment feel less strange.

questions.q: For several months a welder has felt drained and cynical about work, and even weekends do not help him recover. What is this most likely to be?
o: Normal tiredness after a busy week
Burnout from long-term stress
Positive pressure from a deadline
Heat stress from one hot afternoon
questions.why: Burnout is the worn-out, drained feeling that builds when stress goes on for a long time. It needs action: talk to the supervisor and a health professional, and deal with the causes.

questions.q: A worker's employer has an employee assistance programme (EAP). What does it usually offer?
o: Extra pay for staff who work overtime
Free, confidential counselling and advice
A loan scheme run by the supervisor
Time off whenever a worker feels stressed
questions.why: An EAP is a service the employer pays for, so staff can talk privately to a counsellor about work or personal problems. The employer is not told what was said.

questions.q: A co-worker comes back after his grandmother's funeral. He is quiet and slow and has made two mistakes. What is the most helpful thing his supervisor can do?
o: Give him a written warning about both of the mistakes straight away
Tell the team to leave him completely alone for the next month
Give him extra work so that his mind is kept off his loss
Check in privately, ease his load for a while, and mention support
questions.why: Grief is a major stressor. A private word, a short-term change in workload and pointing to support, such as an EAP or a counsellor, help him recover and keep the work safe.

questions.q: Which weekly routine meets common health advice on exercise for adults?
o: A brisk 30-minute walk on five days a week
One 45-minute game of football once a week
Two 20-minute walks spread across the week
A 10-minute stretch every morning before work
questions.why: Health guides commonly advise at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, and 5 × 30 minutes is 150. Regular exercise burns off stress hormones and improves mood and sleep.
